newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: FEATURE - Idyllic African isle seeks loving owner.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Idyllic African isle seeks loving owner.

text.p: Sailfish and marlin play in the indigo depths off this palm-fringed Indian Ocean island. Turtles wallow in its warm, translucent shallows through darting clouds of brilliant fish.
Beyond the coral-white beaches, shimmering in the scorching light, the ragged sails of native dhows silently brush the horizon.

Paradise rises gently from the blue sea, verdant and still in the steaming heat. Quiet crabs nibble at its miniature mangrove swamp and snowy white egrets flap their wings to cool off in the treetops.

The visitor feels swept away, marooned off a lonely coast. But for a certain kind of traveller it's the perfect quiet spot for diving, snorkelling and game-fishing, laid-back, uncrowded and far off the beaten track.
And it's for sale, asking price $3.5 million.
There's no phone, no TV, not a single car. Just a breathtakingly brief and crumbling airstrip, a ruined stone fort, and a rundown hotel complex from a Graham Greene novel.

Once a playground for rich white Rhodesians and South Africans, the classic 1950's architecture of the resort peeled and rusted into a state of genteel ruin while Mozambique fought for liberation from Portugal then plunged into civil war.

In 1993, Mozambique privatised the island, then known as Santa Carolina, and South African businessman Richard Makin won the tender for a 99-year lease, tied to tourist development in keeping with the island group's status as a marine nature reserve.
ISLAND HOTEL EVOKES MEMORIES OF HAVANA

The main hotel is crisply defined in white and blue and pastels, with its graceful 50's terrace overhanging a rocky cove. Inside there's a dark, cool woodpanelled bar and spartan bedrooms fitted with mosquito nets and cold showers.

There are bungalows reminiscent of Havana's paint-peeling villas, a jetty with broken steps, a servants' barracks wreathed with the smoke of cooking fires. Aside from the low rumble of an electricity generator, there's only the dry rattle of palm fronds and the occasional thump of a falling coconut.

"It's like being in paradise. You walk out of the hotel, down to the beach, out to the reef and start snorkeling. It's fantastic," said Attila Csernus, a deeply tanned South African ending a week's stay.
Jimmy Doyle, who brought his wife and two teenaged sons, said he had already booked for another week in October.
"The accomodation's very basic but the island is unique. If you want luxury you won't be happy, but if you love the outdoors, the sea and the reef there's no place like it."

Paradise lies about 10 km (six miles) off the coast of central Mozambique. It is served via twice weekly flights from the capital, Maputo, by a Czech-built 17-seat plane which needs all of its short-takeoff-landing attributes to make the trip.

The plane is called Fluffy, by the way, and on a recent visit passengers leaving the island had to disembark to push it out of a pothole in the runway, an ancient skin of concrete with the consistency of broken biscuits.
But this is not mass tourism, and Makin's resident manager, Portuguese-speaking Antonio Alves, is confident the strip will be fine with a coat of asphalt and a little extension out to sea.
MANAGER HAD BRUISING LEGAL TUSSLE
Once they're fixed up, Paradise Island will have 200 breezy, high-ceilinged bedrooms to offer, with grilled barracuda and cajun-fried calamari for lunch.
"They're not making real estate like this any more," says Makin. "It's beautiful. It's unique."

For four years, he flew his own plane to the island from South Africa, and ferried building materials to its sandy beaches by boat. Now, embittered by what he says was an exhausting legal tussle with the Mozambique government, he intends to sell.
"At one point they sent the army to evict us at gunpoint, but eventually we won and in a Mozambique court, which I'll never forget," he told Reuters.

Makin says he learned a lot about doing business with a formerly communist government trying to intrduce the free market in what is technically one of the world's poorest countries, and he implied not all of the lesson was pleasant.
He admitted he was not entirely blameless in the dispute, apparently over honouring the terms of his 99-year lease.
There was no For Sale sign planted under a canopy of shade trees along the cracked walk from one side of the three km-long (1.5 mile) island to the other, 500 metres (yards) away.

But a brooding atmosphere of uncertainty hung over the Mozambican staff. Painting, scraping and sweeping away at the hotel's gradual renovation, or serving up ice-cold beers to the few sunburned guests on the terrace, they seemed to wonder if the island now would ever recover its lost glory.
Upstairs, a soft Indian Ocean breeze blew through open windows over an old parquet floor smoothed by dancers from a bygone era.
It was easy to imagine ghostly music playing in the empty ballroom, and at its abandoned bar, fantastically curved and fashioned when formica was the rage, some lounging Mastroianni.
Paradise seemed lost, but with a charm all its own.
